tagline: Paul's letter to a gifted, divided, and very Roman church, answering its quarrels and questions with the message of Christ crucified and risen.
overview:
First Corinthians is a real letter written to a real congregation with real problems, and that is what makes it so useful. The church in Corinth was only a few years old. It was rich in spiritual gifts and eloquent speech, and it was coming apart. Members were lining up behind favorite leaders, suing one another in pagan courts, tolerating a scandalous sexual relationship, arguing about marriage and celibacy, eating in pagan temples, humiliating poorer members at the Lord's Supper, competing over spiritual gifts, and doubting the resurrection of the body. Paul answers each problem in turn, first the troubles he has heard about by report, then the questions the Corinthians had put to him in a letter of their own.

What holds the letter together is not a list of rules but a single center. Paul keeps bringing every issue back to the cross, where God showed his wisdom and power in what the world counted weakness and foolishness, and to the resurrection, where God showed that the body and the future matter. Along the way the letter gives the church some of its most loved and most used passages: the account of the Lord's Supper in chapter 11, the picture of the church as one body with many members in chapter 12, the chapter on love in chapter 13, and the earliest written summary of the gospel and the resurrection appearances in chapter 15.

The letter matters because the Corinthian church looks so much like churches in every age. It was proud of its knowledge and blind to its divisions. It mixed the gospel with the status games of its city. Paul does not abandon the congregation, and he does not flatter it. He calls it holy while telling it plainly where it has gone wrong, which is a model of pastoral honesty in its own right.
author: The letter names Paul as its author, with "our brother Sosthenes" as co-sender (1:1). Paul's authorship is not seriously disputed by scholars of any school; 1 Corinthians belongs to the small group of letters that nearly everyone accepts as Paul's own. It is also one of the earliest Christian writings to be quoted by name: the letter known as 1 Clement, sent from the church in Rome to the church in Corinth around AD 96, reminds the Corinthians of what the apostle Paul had written to them about factions. Sosthenes may be the synagogue ruler of that name who was beaten in Corinth in Acts 18:17, though the name was common and the identification cannot be proved. Paul dictated at least part of the letter, since he adds a greeting in his own hand at the end (16:21). Some scholars have proposed that 1 Corinthians combines more than one of Paul's letters, but most regard it as a single letter, and its shifts of subject are explained by the fact that Paul is answering a list of separate questions.
date: Paul wrote 1 Corinthians from Ephesus, on the west coast of Asia Minor (modern Turkey), where he says he will stay "until Pentecost" (16:8). He had founded the Corinthian church a few years earlier, during a stay of about eighteen months described in Acts 18. That stay can be dated with unusual confidence, because Acts 18:12 says Paul was brought before Gallio, the Roman governor of Achaia, and an inscription found at Delphi places Gallio's term of office around AD 51 to 52. Paul then spent between two and three years in Ephesus (Acts 19:8-10; 20:31). First Corinthians comes from that period, most likely around AD 53 to 55. It was not Paul's first letter to the church: he mentions an earlier letter that has not survived (5:9). Second Corinthians, written later from Macedonia, shows that the relationship went through further strain after this letter was sent.
setting:
Corinth sat on the narrow isthmus that joins mainland Greece to the Peloponnese, with a port on each side: Lechaeum on the Corinthian Gulf to the west and Cenchreae on the Saronic Gulf to the east. Cargo and even small ships were hauled across the isthmus on a paved trackway, so trade from east and west passed through the city. The old Greek city had been destroyed by the Roman general Lucius Mummius in 146 BC. In 44 BC Julius Caesar refounded it as a Roman colony, settled largely with freed slaves and veterans, and it became the capital of the Roman province of Achaia. The Corinth that Paul knew was therefore a Roman city in Greece, laid out on Roman lines, with Latin as its official language and a population that included Greeks, Romans, Jews, and people from across the eastern Mediterranean.

It was a city where status could be won. Freedmen and merchants rose to wealth, sponsored public buildings, and had their generosity recorded in inscriptions; a paving stone near the theater records that an Erastus laid the pavement at his own expense in return for his office, and some identify him with the Erastus of Romans 16:23. The Isthmian Games, one of the great athletic festivals of Greece, were held nearby every two years. Temples to Apollo, Aphrodite, Asclepius the healing god, and the imperial family stood in and around the city, and meals in temple dining rooms were part of ordinary civic and social life. Orators and teachers of rhetoric drew crowds and followers. An often repeated claim that a temple of Aphrodite kept a thousand sacred prostitutes goes back to the geographer Strabo and describes the older Greek city; many historians doubt that it applied to Roman Corinth. What is clear is that the church Paul wrote to lived surrounded by idols, patronage, competition for honor, and a relaxed sexual ethic, and it had brought much of that world into its own gatherings.
purpose: Paul wrote to restore a divided church to the gospel it had received. He had heard reports from "Chloe's household" about quarrels (1:11) and other news about immorality and lawsuits (5:1; 6:1). He had also received a letter from the church asking a series of questions, and three members, Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus, had come to him (16:17). The first part of the letter (chapters 1 to 6) deals with what he has heard. The second part answers the Corinthians' own questions, each introduced with the phrase "now concerning" or a close variant (7:1; 7:25; 8:1; 12:1; 16:1; 16:12). Through it all Paul aims at unity, holiness, and love: a church that builds up its weakest members instead of prizing its most impressive ones, and that waits for the resurrection rather than acting as if it had already arrived. He also prepares the church for the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem (16:1-4) and for his coming visit.
story: The founding of the Corinthian church is told in Acts 18, during Paul's second missionary campaign. After preaching in Athens, Paul came to Corinth, worked as a tentmaker alongside Aquila and Priscilla, preached in the synagogue, and then moved next door to the house of Titius Justus when he met opposition. Crispus, the synagogue ruler, believed with his household. After Paul left, the Alexandrian teacher Apollos ministered in Corinth (Acts 18:24-19:1). First Corinthians belongs to the next stage, Paul's long stay in Ephesus during his third campaign. In the larger story of the Bible, the letter shows the promise to Abraham reaching the nations: a church of Jews and Gentiles in a pagan Roman city, told “you yourselves are God’s temple” (3:16), learning what it means to be the holy people of God without a temple of stone, a land, or a king other than Christ.
christ: The letter is Christ-centered in the most literal way. Paul resolved to know nothing among the Corinthians "except Jesus Christ and Him crucified" (2:2), and the cross becomes the measure of wisdom, leadership, freedom, and worship. Christ is the foundation of the church (3:11), the Passover lamb who has been sacrificed (5:7), the one Lord through whom all things exist (8:6), the one whose body and blood the church shares at the Supper (10:16; 11:23-26), and the one whose body the believers are, each of them a member of it (12:12-27). Chapter 15 gives the fullest account in the New Testament of Christ's resurrection and its meaning: he died for our sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, was raised on the third day, and appeared to many witnesses, and his resurrection is the firstfruits of the resurrection of all who belong to him. Christ is also the last Adam, the head of a new humanity, who will hand the kingdom over to the Father when every enemy, death included, is destroyed.
reading: Read 1 Corinthians as one side of a conversation. Paul sometimes quotes the Corinthians' own slogans before answering them, and many translations mark phrases such as "Everything is permissible for me" (6:12) as Corinthian sayings Paul is qualifying. Readers disagree about where some of these quotations begin and end, and those decisions shape the meaning of several passages. Pay attention to the division between the reports of chapters 1 to 6 and the "now concerning" questions from chapter 7 onward. Several topics, such as head coverings, the silence of women in 14:34-35 (which some manuscripts place after 14:40), speaking in tongues, and the meaning of baptism for the dead in 15:29, are genuinely difficult and disputed; the notes set out the main views. A common misreading takes the love chapter as a wedding reading detached from its setting. In context it is a rebuke to a church competing over spiritual gifts, and it describes the love that should govern worship and community life.

structure.title: Greeting and thanksgiving
structure.summary: Paul greets the church as God's holy people and thanks God for its gifts, while pointing ahead to the day of Christ that it must still wait for.

structure.title: Divisions and the wisdom of the cross
structure.summary: Paul answers the reports of factions gathered around leaders. The message of the crucified Christ overturns the world's wisdom and status, and leaders are only servants and stewards of God.

structure.title: Immorality, lawsuits, and the body
structure.summary: Paul confronts a case of incest the church has tolerated, rebukes members for suing one another before pagan courts, and teaches that the body belongs to the Lord and is a temple of the Holy Spirit.

structure.title: Marriage, singleness, and calling
structure.summary: Answering the Corinthians' first question, Paul discusses sexual relations within marriage, divorce, mixed marriages, and the value of remaining single in a time of pressure.

structure.title: Food offered to idols and the use of freedom
structure.summary: Paul addresses eating food sacrificed to idols. Knowledge must give way to love for the weaker brother, Paul gives up his own rights for the gospel, and the church must flee idolatry.

structure.title: Order in worship and the Lord's Supper
structure.summary: Paul addresses head coverings in worship and then rebukes the church for meals where the rich eat while the poor go hungry, handing on the tradition of the Lord's Supper.

structure.title: Spiritual gifts and the way of love
structure.summary: The Spirit gives varied gifts to one body for the common good. Love is the greater way, and worship should be orderly and intelligible so that everyone is built up.

structure.title: The resurrection of the dead
structure.summary: Paul restates the gospel of Christ's death, burial, resurrection, and appearances, argues that the resurrection of believers depends on it, and describes the resurrection body and the final defeat of death.

structure.title: The collection, travel plans, and greetings
structure.summary: Paul gives instructions for the collection for Jerusalem, shares his plans, commends coworkers, and closes with greetings in his own hand.

themes.title: The wisdom of the cross
themes.body: Corinth prized eloquence, knowledge, and status, and the church had carried those values into its life. Paul answers that God has shown his wisdom in a crucified Messiah, a message that looked foolish to Greeks and offensive to Jews. The cross does not only save; it reorders what counts as strength, honor, and wisdom, and Paul applies it to leadership, lawsuits, freedom, and worship.

themes.title: One body, one temple
themes.body: Paul describes the church as God's field, God's building, God's temple, and the body of Christ. These pictures all make the same point: the believers belong to God and to one another, and division is not a matter of taste but an attack on what God is building. Unity does not mean sameness; the body has many members with different gifts, and the weaker ones are indispensable.

themes.title: Holiness in the body
themes.body: Some Corinthians seem to have thought that what they did with their bodies did not touch their spiritual life. Paul insists the reverse. The body belongs to the Lord, is a temple of the Holy Spirit, and will be raised. Sexual conduct, food, and worship are therefore matters of holiness, and the church is called to be different from its city without withdrawing from it.

themes.title: Love that builds up
themes.body: Again and again Paul sets knowledge that puffs up against love that builds up. The strong are to limit their freedom for the sake of the weak, gifts are to serve the common good, and the Supper is to be shared, not hoarded. Chapter 13 gathers this theme into its most famous form: without love, even the most impressive gifts amount to nothing.

themes.title: Resurrection and the not yet
themes.body: Parts of the church behaved as if they had already arrived, rich and reigning. Paul reminds them that the end has not come: they still wait for the revelation of Christ, the day of judgment, and the resurrection of the body. Chapter 15 grounds Christian hope in Christ's bodily resurrection and makes it the reason that labor in the Lord is not in vain.

keyChapters.why: Sets out the letter's center: the message of the cross as God's power and wisdom, confronting a church divided by loyalty to leaders.
Leaders are servants and fellow workers, Christ is the only foundation, and the church is God's holy temple where his Spirit dwells.
Paul's longest discussion of marriage, singleness, and divorce, shaped by the conviction that the present form of the world is passing away.
On food sacrificed to idols, Paul sets knowledge against love and confesses one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ.
Contains the earliest written account of Jesus instituting the Lord's Supper, set in a rebuke of a divided church meal.
The Spirit gives varied gifts to one body for the common good, and every member, especially the weaker, is needed.
The chapter on love, which judges every gift and every claim to knowledge by whether it is patient, kind, and humble.
The fullest New Testament teaching on the resurrection of Christ and of believers, and the earliest written list of resurrection appearances.

parts.body:
1 Corinthians is a letter. Paul wrote it to the followers of Jesus in Corinth, a busy Roman city in southern Greece, a few years after he had started the church there. It has 16 chapters.

It is a real letter to a real church with real trouble. The church was young, gifted and proud, and it was coming apart. Members lined up behind favourite leaders. One man was living with his father's wife, and the church did nothing. Believers took one another to court. Some said the body did not matter. Others asked whether married people should stop sleeping together. Some ate meals in the temples of other gods. At the Lord's Supper the rich ate well while the poor went hungry. People competed over spiritual gifts. And some said there would be no resurrection of the dead.

Paul answers each problem in turn. But he does not answer with a list of rules. He keeps bringing every question back to one centre: Jesus Christ crucified and raised. He says so near the start: “For I resolved to know nothing while I was with you except Jesus Christ and Him crucified” (2:2).

So the letter moves from the cross to the resurrection. It begins with the message of the cross, which looks foolish to the world and is God's power. It ends with the longest chapter in the New Testament on the rising of the dead. Between them come marriage and singleness, money and status, food and worship, gifts and love.

Many of the Bible's best known passages are here: the church as one body with many parts (chapter 12), the chapter on love (chapter 13), the words Jesus spoke over the bread and cup (11:23-26), and the earliest written list of people who saw Jesus risen (15:3-8).

The church in Corinth looks a great deal like churches in every age. It was proud of what it knew and blind to its divisions. It had brought its city's love of status into its own meetings. Paul does not give up on it and he does not flatter it. He calls it holy while he tells it plainly where it has gone wrong. That is why the letter still speaks.

The letter names its writer at once: “Paul, called to be an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and our brother Sosthenes” (1:1). An apostle is someone sent with a message. Paul had founded the church in Corinth himself.

Almost no one doubts that Paul wrote it. Scholars of every school count 1 Corinthians among the letters that are surely his own. It is also one of the first Christian writings that another early writer names. Near the end of the first century the church in Rome sent a letter to the church in Corinth, known today as 1 Clement. It tells the Corinthians to take up the letter of the apostle Paul and remember what he wrote to them about himself, Cephas and Apollos, because even then they had split into parties. So about forty years later the church in Corinth still had the letter and still needed it.

Sosthenes is named beside Paul. Acts tells of a Sosthenes who led the synagogue in Corinth and was beaten in front of the governor's seat (Acts 18:17). Some think this is the same man, now a believer. The name was common, so that is not certain.

Paul did not write every word with his own pen. Like other letter writers of his day he spoke and someone else wrote. At the end he takes the pen himself: “This greeting is in my own hand” (16:21). A greeting in the writer's own hand was a personal touch, and a guard against forged letters.

The letter is full of Paul's own voice. He is by turns tender and sharp, ironic and grieving. He calls himself their father in the faith (4:15). He tells them what he has suffered. He admits he came to them “in weakness and fear, and with much trembling” (2:3). He also marks carefully when he passes on a command of Jesus and when he gives his own judgment (7:10, 7:12, 7:25). Few letters let us hear a pastor think so openly.

Some scholars have suggested that the letter as we have it joins more than one of Paul's letters together. Most read it as one letter. Its sudden changes of subject are explained by what it is: an answer to a list of separate questions.

parts.h: When and where it was written
parts.body:
Paul wrote 1 Corinthians from Ephesus, a great city on the west coast of what is now Turkey. He says so himself: “But I will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost” (16:8). Pentecost was a Jewish feast in early summer, so he was most likely writing in the spring.

Acts tells how the church began. Paul came to Corinth after preaching in Athens. He worked as a tentmaker with Aquila and Priscilla, preached in the synagogue, and then moved next door to the house of a man named Titus Justus. He stayed a long time: “So Paul stayed for a year and a half, teaching the word of God among the Corinthians” (Acts 18:11).

That stay can be dated better than almost anything else in Paul's life. In Corinth Paul was brought before Gallio, the Roman governor of Achaia, the province of southern Greece (Acts 18:12). At Delphi in Greece, pieces of a letter from the emperor Claudius were found cut in stone, and the letter names Gallio as governor. It fixes his year in office. Most scholars place it in AD 51 to 52; some say 50 to 51. Paul's first stay in Corinth was around then.

After that Paul travelled east and then came back to Ephesus. He stayed there two to three years (Acts 19:10; 20:31). 1 Corinthians belongs to that time. Most place it about AD 53 to 55. That is only some twenty to twenty-five years after Jesus died and rose.

So the letter is one of the earliest pieces of the New Testament. When Paul passes on the words of Jesus over the bread and cup, or the list of those who saw him risen, he is writing within living memory. He even says that most of the more than five hundred who saw Jesus at once “are still living” (15:6).

It was not Paul's first letter to Corinth. He mentions an earlier one that has been lost (5:9). Nor was it his last. 2 Corinthians, written later from Macedonia in northern Greece, shows that the story went on.

Corinth stood on a narrow neck of land that joins mainland Greece to the large peninsula to its south. It had a harbour on each side: Lechaeum on the gulf to the west and Cenchrea on the gulf to the east. Trade between east and west passed through it. Corinth lived on that trade.

There had been a famous Greek Corinth long before. The Romans destroyed it in 146 BC, and it lay mostly empty for about a century. Then in 44 BC Julius Caesar founded it again as a Roman colony, a city of Roman citizens planted abroad. The geographer Strabo says it was settled largely with freed slaves; some historians think the settlers were more mixed than that from the start. By Paul's day it was the seat of the Roman governor of Achaia.

So the Corinth Paul knew was not an old Greek town. It was a new Roman city in Greece, about a hundred years old, laid out on Roman lines, with Latin on its official inscriptions and Greek in its streets. People came from all over the eastern Mediterranean. There was a Jewish community with its synagogue (Acts 18:4).

It was a place where people could rise. Freed slaves and traders grew rich. Wealthy citizens paid for public works and had their gifts cut in stone. A paving stone found near the theatre in 1929 says that an Erastus laid the pavement at his own expense in return for his office. In a letter written from Corinth, Paul sends greetings from “Erastus, the city treasurer” (Romans 16:23). Some think they are the same man; others doubt it, and the date of the pavement is argued. The stone shows the kind of city it was: a city hungry for honour.

Temples to many gods stood in and around the city, and meals in temple dining rooms were part of ordinary social life. The Isthmian Games, one of the great festivals of Greek sport, held every two years in honour of the sea god Poseidon, belonged to Corinth. Speakers and teachers drew crowds and followers.

Corinth is often pictured as a city of vice. Much of that picture rests on one famous claim: that a temple of the goddess Aphrodite in Corinth kept more than a thousand temple prostitutes. That claim comes from the geographer Strabo, who seems to have been describing the older Greek city, before 146 BC. Many historians doubt it, and it tells us little or nothing about the Roman city of Paul's day. What is clear from the letter itself is enough: the church lived among idols, patrons, competition for honour and a relaxed view of sex, and it had brought much of that into its own life.

Who were the Christians in Corinth? Paul tells them to look at themselves: “Brothers, consider the time of your calling: Not many of you were wise by human standards; not many were powerful; not many were of noble birth” (1:26).

Not many. But some. The names in the letter and in Acts show a mixed church. Crispus had led the synagogue (1:14; Acts 18:8). Gaius later hosted “all the church” (Romans 16:23), so he must have had a large house. Stephanas and his household were the first believers in the region (16:15). Chloe had people who travelled between Corinth and Ephesus (1:11). Alongside them were many with little: workers, the poor, and slaves, whom Paul speaks to directly (7:21-23).

Most of the believers were Gentiles, people who were not Jews. Paul reminds them that they used to be “led astray to mute idols” (12:2). Some were Jews. Paul writes to both, and he says in Christ they were baptized into one body, “whether Jews or Greeks, slave or free” (12:13).

There were no church buildings. The believers met in homes. A house church met in the home of a host, often a person of means, who acted as its patron. A patron was someone of standing who gave help and protection and was owed honour in return. That pattern helps explain many of the letter's troubles. Some historians who have studied houses dug up near Corinth think a dining room could hold only a few guests lying on couches, with the rest outside in the courtyard. Whatever the room, the church could be sorted by rank before anyone said a word. Paul's anger about the Lord's Supper in chapter 11 is aimed at exactly that.

The church was also gifted. Paul thanks God that “you do not lack any spiritual gift” (1:7). They spoke in tongues, prophesied, taught and healed. But gifts became one more way to rank people.

So the divisions in Corinth were not only about ideas. They ran along the lines of the city: rich and poor, educated and not, patron and client, the impressive and the plain. Paul's answer is that the cross has turned those lines upside down. God “chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise” (1:27).

Paul had heard news, and he had received a letter. Both lie behind 1 Corinthians.

The news came first. “My brothers, some from Chloe’s household have informed me that there are quarrels among you” (1:11). Chloe's people were probably members of her household, perhaps slaves or workers, travelling between the two cities. Other reports had reached Paul too: “It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you” (5:1).

Then there was a letter from the church. Paul turns to it in chapter 7: “Now for the matters you wrote about” (7:1). Three men from Corinth had come to Paul: “I am glad that Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus have arrived” (16:17). Many think they brought the letter.

Paul had already written to Corinth once before: “I wrote you in my letter not to associate with sexually immoral people” (5:9). That earlier letter is lost. The Corinthians had taken it to mean they should keep away from every immoral person in the city, and Paul now says what he meant (5:9-13).

How do 1 and 2 Corinthians fit together? Only in broad strokes can anyone say. Paul wrote a first letter, now lost. Then he wrote 1 Corinthians. Afterwards things grew worse. 2 Corinthians speaks of a “painful visit” (2 Corinthians 2:1) and of a letter written “through many tears” (2 Corinthians 2:4). Many scholars think that tearful letter came between 1 and 2 Corinthians and is also lost; others think part of it may survive inside 2 Corinthians, perhaps in chapters 10 to 13. Many scholars think 2 Corinthians itself joins more than one letter, while others read it as one. So Paul may have written four letters or more to Corinth, and the Bible keeps two. Here the evidence is thin, and these notes do not choose.

What is plain is the relationship. Paul stayed with this church through years of trouble. He corrected it, grieved over it, visited it and wrote to it again and again. The two letters in the Bible are part of a long and costly friendship.

1 Corinthians has a clear shape once you see two things.

First, there are two halves. In chapters 1 to 6 Paul answers what he has heard by report: the quarrels over leaders, the man living with his father's wife, the lawsuits, and the use of prostitutes. In chapters 7 to 16 he answers the questions the Corinthians wrote to him.

Second, the questions are marked. Paul opens several of them with the same words, ‘Now about’, which translate the Greek peri de. “Now for the matters you wrote about” (7:1). “Now about virgins” (7:25). “Now about food sacrificed to idols” (8:1). “Now about spiritual gifts” (12:1). “Now about the collection for the saints” (16:1). “Now about our brother Apollos” (16:12). Readers can follow the letter by those signposts.

Here is the outline in one view.

1:1-9. Greeting and thanks.
1:10 to 4:21. Divisions over leaders, and the wisdom of the cross.
Chapters 5 and 6. A case of incest, lawsuits, and the body.
Chapter 7. Marriage, singleness and divorce.
8:1 to 11:1. Food offered to idols, and giving up rights for others.
11:2-34. Head coverings in worship, and the Lord's Supper.
Chapters 12 to 14. Spiritual gifts, love, and order in worship.
Chapter 15. The resurrection of the dead.
Chapter 16. The collection for Jerusalem, travel plans and greetings.

Look at where it begins and ends. It begins with the cross (chapters 1 and 2) and ends with the resurrection (chapter 15). Everything in between is held between those two.

Paul also writes in the style of a debate. Several times he quotes a saying the Corinthians used and then answers it. In 6:12 the Berean Standard Bible prints “Everything is permissible for me” in quotation marks, as a slogan Paul then corrects: “but not everything is beneficial” (6:12). Many translators think 7:1, 8:1 and 8:4 also quote the Corinthians' own words. Greek manuscripts had no quotation marks, so these are judgments by translators, and they differ in places. Where one begins and ends can change the meaning. The chapter notes say where this matters.

The cross as God's wisdom. Corinth prized clever speech, learning and status. Paul answers with a crucified Messiah. Crucifixion was the death Rome kept for slaves and rebels, the most shameful death the empire knew. Paul says, “we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles” (1:23). Yet to those God calls, Christ is “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1:24). The cross does more than save. It turns the world's ideas of strength and honour upside down. Paul applies that to leaders, lawsuits, food, the Supper and gifts.

The body. Paul uses the word ‘body’ in more than one way, and the ways meet. The believer's own body matters: “Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you” (6:19). The church is a body: “Now you are the body of Christ, and each of you is a member of it” (12:27). The bread of the Supper is a sharing in the body of Christ (10:16). And the body will be raised. Some in Corinth thought what you did with your body did not touch your soul. Paul says the opposite. God made the body, Christ bought it, the Spirit lives in it, and God will raise it.

Love. Again and again Paul sets knowledge that makes people proud against love that builds others up: “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (8:1). The strong should give up their freedom for the sake of the weak. Gifts are given “for the common good” (12:7). Chapter 13 gathers all of this together. It is not first a wedding reading. It was written to a church competing over gifts, to say that without love the greatest gift is worth nothing: “If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am only a ringing gong or a clanging cymbal” (13:1).

The resurrection. Some in Corinth said “there is no resurrection of the dead” (15:12). Paul answers with the gospel he had received and passed on: Christ died, was buried, was raised and appeared (15:3-8). He says everything hangs on it: “And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile; you are still in your sins” (15:17). Then he describes the raised body, imperishable, glorious and full of power. Some Corinthians acted as if they had already arrived. Paul reminds them that the end has not yet come. They still wait.

Unity and holiness belong with these. The church is God's field, God's building, God's temple and Christ's body. To divide it is not a matter of taste. And the church is holy, set apart for God, called to live differently from its city without leaving it.

The church in Corinth was mostly Gentile, but Paul teaches it from Israel's Scriptures as from its own Bible. He quotes them often, sometimes in words close to the old Greek translation that Greek-speaking Jews used. That is why his wording does not always match the Old Testament in an English Bible, which is translated from the Hebrew.

He uses the prophets to show that God has always overturned human pride. Isaiah 29:14 stands behind “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise” (1:19). Jeremiah 9:24 stands behind “Let him who boasts boast in the Lord” (1:31). Job 5:13 and Psalm 94:11 are quoted at 3:19-20.

He reads Israel's story as a warning to the church. In chapter 10 he tells of the people in the wilderness, who passed through the sea, ate manna and still fell into idolatry. “Now these things happened to them as examples and were written down as warnings for us” (10:11). He calls them “our forefathers” (10:1), though most of his readers were Gentiles. In Christ they had been joined to Israel's story.

He draws on the law of Moses for the church's life. The case of the man with his father's wife falls under Leviticus 18:8. The command to remove him echoes the refrain of Deuteronomy, “So you must purge the evil from among you” (Deuteronomy 17:7). Christ is “our Passover lamb” (5:7), the lamb of Exodus 12. Genesis 2:24 lies behind his words on sex: “The two will become one flesh” (6:16).

And he hears the Psalms and the prophets speaking of the end. In chapter 15 Psalm 110 and Psalm 8 speak of all enemies put under Christ's feet (15:25-27). Genesis 2:7 speaks of the first Adam, set beside Christ, “the last Adam” (15:45). Isaiah 25:8 and Hosea 13:14 give the letter its last shout over death (15:54-55).

Most of all, he confesses Israel's God. When he writes “there is but one God” (8:6), he is echoing the great confession of Israel: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One” (Deuteronomy 6:4). The note on chapter 8 says what he does with it.

1 Corinthians is often read in ways that make it say less, or more, than it does.

It is not a church manual lifted out of its setting. It is one side of a conversation. Paul answers questions we do not have in full, about situations he could assume and we have to piece together. That is why some passages are hard. Head coverings in worship (11:2-16), women keeping silent (14:34-35), and baptism for the dead (15:29) all turn on details the first readers knew and we do not.

So readers have to decide what was for Corinth and what is for every church. All Christians make that decision, whether they say so or not. Almost no church today forbids eating meat that might have come from a pagan temple, but every church keeps the Lord's Supper. Readers weigh several things. Does Paul ground his words in creation, in the gospel or in the teaching of Jesus, or in the custom of the day? Does he say ‘in all the churches’ (7:17; 14:33)? Is this his own judgment, which he marks as such (7:25)? How do the rest of Scripture and the long memory of the church read it?

Faithful Christians weigh those things differently, and they reach different answers on some questions, such as head coverings, gifts like tongues, and the place of women in leading worship. The chapter notes set out the main views fairly and do not choose where faithful churches differ.

It is not a book of rules for punishing people. Paul does tell the church to act in a case of serious sin (chapter 5). But he limits that to the church's own members, never the world outside (5:12-13), and he aims at the person's rescue (5:5). He never asks the church to shield a wrongdoer or to silence someone who has been harmed.

It is not anti-body or anti-sex. Paul is careful to say that marriage is good and that sex within marriage is a shared gift and duty (7:3-5). He honours singleness too, as a gift and not a lesser life (7:7).

And it is not a letter for winners. Its heroes are not the impressive. They are the weak believer “for whom Christ died” (8:11), the poor who went hungry at the Supper, and the parts of the body that “seem to be weaker” (12:22). The letter's last word on gifts and knowledge is love.

Read it as a letter. Begin at the beginning and read a long piece at a sitting. Chapters 1 to 4 belong together, and so do 8 to 10 and 12 to 14. A verse makes most sense inside its argument.

Read it as one side of a conversation. Ask, as you go, what the Corinthians must have been saying or doing to draw this answer. Notice where Paul seems to quote them and then turn their words.

Read it with the city in mind. Corinth was proud, new, mixed and hungry for status. Much of what sounds odd becomes clear when you picture a house church where a patron, a merchant, a slave and a former synagogue leader shared one meal.

Read the hard passages slowly and humbly. Some questions in this letter have been argued for centuries by careful readers on every side. The notes on each chapter set out the main readings fairly. They do not ask you to settle what faithful churches have not settled.

Read it for its centre. Every question in the letter, from lawsuits to food to worship, is answered from the cross and the resurrection. Ask of each chapter: what does the crucified and risen Lord have to do with this?

And read it for yourself. The church in Corinth was gifted, divided and proud, and it did not know it. Paul's question still lands on any reader: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (4:7).

hard.line: ‘Christ did not send me to baptize’. What Paul means about baptism, and why it does not make baptism unimportant.
‘Saved, but only as if through the flames’. How Catholics and Protestants each read the testing fire.
‘Hand this man over to Satan’. What it most likely means, how churches practise discipline, and how it must never be used.
The list of those who will not inherit the kingdom, and the two Greek words joined in one phrase. What Paul says, how Christians read it, and ‘that is what some of you were’.
Divorce and remarriage: what Jesus said, what Paul adds, and how churches read ‘not bound’. Nothing here asks anyone to stay in danger.
A word to slaves that can be translated two ways, set beside ‘do not become slaves of men’.
‘An idol is nothing’, and one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ: Jesus inside Israel's confession of the one God.
Head coverings in worship: what Paul asks, what it meant in Corinth, and how churches read it today.
Eating ‘in an unworthy manner’, and why some were sick. What Paul means by recognizing the body.
‘Women are to be silent in the churches’. The puzzle of these verses beside 11:5, and the views.
‘Baptized for the dead’. One of the most puzzling verses in the Bible, and why its meaning is uncertain.
A curse and a prayer in one verse: ‘Come, O Lord’, an Aramaic prayer left untranslated in a Greek letter.

words.line: Greek sophia. Corinth's wisdom meant clever speech, learning and status. God's wisdom is the crucified Christ, who “has become for us wisdom from God” (1:30).
The most shameful death in the Roman world, kept for slaves and rebels. Paul calls his message “the message of the cross” (1:18): foolish to the world, God's power to those being saved.

Greek pneumatikos, shaped by the Spirit of God. The Corinthians used it to rank themselves. Paul says the truly spiritual person has the Spirit, and that their quarrels show they are not living like it (3:1-3).
Greek psychikos, a person living only by human powers, without the Spirit (2:14). Not wicked in itself, but unable to receive what the Spirit gives.
Greek sarkikos, living by merely human ways. Paul says jealousy and quarrels show it: “Are you not walking in the way of man?” (3:3).
Greek sōma. The believer's own body, a temple of the Spirit (6:19); the church, the body of Christ (12:27); and the body that will be raised (15:44).
Greek gnōsis. The Corinthians prized it. Paul does not despise it, but says “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (8:1).
Greek syneidēsis, the inner sense that judges your own actions. A ‘weak’ conscience is one still troubled by its old life with idols; others must not wound it (8:7-12).
Greek charisma, a gift of grace. Paul uses it for marriage and singleness (7:7) and for the gifts of the Spirit, given “for the common good” (12:7).
Greek agapē, love that seeks another's good at cost to itself. Without it every gift is nothing (13:1-3). Of faith, hope and love, “the greatest of these is love” (13:13).
Greek oikodomeō, to build a house. Paul's test for knowledge, gifts and worship: does it build up the church? (8:1; 14:26).
Greek physioō, to inflate. A favourite word of this letter for the church's swollen pride (4:6; 5:2; 8:1; 13:4).
Greek hagioi, holy ones, people set apart for God. Paul calls the whole troubled church “called to be holy” (1:2). It is not a word for the unusually good.
Greek anastasis, the rising of the dead to bodily life. Christ is “the firstfruits” (15:20), the first of the harvest; those who belong to him will follow.

timeline.what: The Romans destroy the old Greek city of Corinth. It lies mostly empty for about a century.
Julius Caesar founds Corinth again as a Roman colony. It becomes the seat of the governor of Achaia.
Claudius expels Jews from Rome. Aquila and Priscilla come to Corinth (Acts 18:2). The year comes from a later writer.
Paul in Corinth for a year and a half, working with Aquila and Priscilla. The church begins (Acts 18:1-11).
Gallio is governor of Achaia, as an inscription at Delphi shows. Paul is brought before him in Corinth (Acts 18:12).
Apollos, a learned Jew from Alexandria, teaches in Corinth and helps the believers (Acts 18:27-28). Paul later writes, “I planted the seed and Apollos watered it” (3:6).
Paul writes an earlier letter to Corinth, now lost (5:9).
Paul teaches at Ephesus for two to three years (Acts 19:10; 20:31). News comes from Chloe's household, and a letter from Corinth.
Paul writes 1 Corinthians from Ephesus, in the spring, meaning to stay “until Pentecost” (16:8).
A painful visit to Corinth and a letter written “through many tears” (2 Corinthians 2:1-4), probably lost. Then 2 Corinthians, from Macedonia.
Paul spends three months in Greece (Acts 20:2-3), most likely at Corinth, and writes Romans there, before taking the collection to Jerusalem.
The church in Rome writes to the church in Corinth (1 Clement), reminding it of what Paul wrote about its parties.

places.name: Corinth
places.line: Where the letter went: a Roman colony on the narrow neck of land in southern Greece, where Paul had started the church (1:2). Chloe's people brought him news of it (1:11).

places.name: Ephesus
places.line: Where Paul wrote, planning to stay “until Pentecost” because a great door for work had opened (16:8-9). Aquila and Prisca send greetings from here (16:19).

places.name: Jerusalem
places.line: Where the collection for the poor believers was to go. Corinth's own messengers would carry the gift (16:3).

teaching.mapNote: The letter was written at Ephesus and sent across the Aegean Sea to Corinth. Cenchrea, Corinth's eastern harbour, lies just east of the city, too close to draw apart on a map this size. Paul planned to come by land through Macedonia, in northern Greece (16:5), and the gift was to go to Jerusalem (16:3).
